q-160402:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={e}^{u-v}$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(uv).$  

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u-v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-{e}^{u-v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\frac{1}{u} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{v}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{u-v} & -{e}^{u-v} \\ \frac{1}{u} & \frac{1}{v}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u-v}\cdot (\frac{1}{v})-(-{e}^{u-v})\cdot \frac{1}{u} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{u-v}}{v}+\frac{{e}^{u-v}}{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(1,1)}=\frac{{e}^{(1)-(1)}}{(1)}+\frac{{e}^{(1)-(1)}}{(1)}=2.
$$

q-160440:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡u$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡v-0\cdot 0 \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\pi /6 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(\frac{\pi }{6},0)}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

q-161877:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{u-v} & -\frac{1}{u-v} \\ -2u & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{u-v}\cdot 1-(-2u)\cdot (-\frac{1}{u-v}) \\  & =\frac{1-2u}{u-v} \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(2,1)} & ={(\frac{1-2u}{u-v})\,|}_{u=2\,v=1} \\  & =\frac{1-2(2)}{2-1} \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-3|\cdot \delta A \\  & =3\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

q-161788:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 1 \\ 2 & -3{v}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-3{v}^{2})-1\cdot 2 \\  & =-6u{v}^{2}-2 \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(1,2)} & =(-6u{v}^{2}-2)\,{|}_{u=1\,v=2} \\  & =-6(1)(2)^{2}-2 \\  & =-26\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-26|\cdot \delta A \\  & =26\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

q-161842:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing at the points where the Jacobian determinant is negative:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}<0
$$

We have

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} \\ u-\frac{1}{3}v\end{aligned}].
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3{u}^{2} & -v \\ 1 & -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}| \\  & =(3{u}^{2})\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})-(1)\cdot (-v) \\  & =v-{u}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}v-{u}^{2} & <0 \\ v & <{u}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that the equation 

$$
v={u}^{2}
$$

defines a parabola, and the coordinates of, say, $(1,-1)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing must be the following:

q-161837:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing at the points where the Jacobian determinant is negative:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}<0
$$

We have

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}+v \\ uv\end{aligned}].
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{u}^{2} & 1 \\ v & u\end{aligned}| \\  & ={u}^{2}\cdot u-v\cdot 1 \\  & ={u}^{3}-v.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{3}-v & <0 \\ v & >{u}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that the equation 

$$
v={u}^{3}
$$

defines a cubic function, and the coordinates of, say, $(-1,1)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing must be the following:

q-131171:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy) \\  & =\frac{1}{x}+x \\  & =\frac{1+{x}^{2}}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-131174:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
∇\cdot F=\text{div}\,F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+\frac{{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\  & =3\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(3,4),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\cdot F)(3,4) & =3\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{9+16} \\  & =3\sqrt{25} \\  & =15.\end{aligned}
$$

q-131179:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x(y{e}^{z}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y))+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{e}^{z})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z(x+1)) \\  & =(y{e}^{z}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y)+x{e}^{z}+(x+1) \\  & =y{e}^{z}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y+x{e}^{z}+x+1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(1,1,0),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\cdot F)(1,1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{0}+\operatorname{ln}⁡1+1\cdot {e}^{0}+1+1 \\  & =1+0+1+1+1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

q-123192:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}yz)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}z)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy{z}^{2}) \\  & =2xyz+2xyz+2xyz \\  & =6xyz.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(1,2,2),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\cdot F)(1,2,2) & =6(1)(2)(2) \\  & =6\cdot 4 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

q-107999:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14108748/assets/017463f3ac8abac9c2b00c4d9a715a4109a5f4bc1b070e0a12c4d3a7bac64351.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $4x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4x.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x=\int 4x\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=2\,\text{m}$ when $v=8\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =2(2)^{2}+C \\ C & =32-8 \\ C & =24\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}+24 \\ {v}^{2} & =4{x}^{2}+48 \\ {v}^{2} & =4({x}^{2}+12) \\ v & =\pm 2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+12}.
$$

q-122325:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14108748/assets/8faba5a783797f7025f51ec1ae587cb68355dff7138278689346c2f713275562.png)

We're given that the velocity function $v(x)$ is

$$
v(x)={e}^{-2x}.
$$

We know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}={e}^{-2x}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & ={e}^{-2x} \\ \frac{1}{{e}^{-2x}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \int {e}^{2x}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \int {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x} & =t+K \\ {e}^{2x} & =2t+C \\ 2x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+C) \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+C)\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1).
$$

q-131338:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the curl of $F$ is the vector field given by

$$
curl\,F=∇\times F=|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{aligned}|.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ x & 2y & 3z\end{aligned}| \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(3z)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(2y)]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(3z)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(x)]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x)]k \\  & =(0-0)\,i-(0-0)\,j+(0-0)\,k \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-98894:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3},$ and the first partial derivatives exist, then the curl of $F$ is the vector field on ${R}^{3}$ defined by

$$
curl\,F=∇\times F=|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{aligned}|.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ 0 & xy{e}^{z} & yz{e}^{x}\end{aligned}| \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(yz{e}^{x})-\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy{e}^{z})]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(yz{e}^{x})-\frac{∂}{∂z}(0)]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{e}^{z})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(0)]k \\  & =(z{e}^{x}-xy{e}^{z})i-(yz{e}^{x}-0)j+(y{e}^{z}-0)k \\  & =(z{e}^{x}-xy{e}^{z})\,i-yz{e}^{x}\,j+y{e}^{z}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{curl}\,F$ at the point $(0,2,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\text{curl}\,F)(0,2,1) & =(1\cdot {e}^{0}-0\cdot 2\cdot {e}^{1})\,i-2\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{0}\,j+2\cdot {e}^{1}\,k \\  & =i-2j+2e\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

q-126520:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $F$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1))-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+1}-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the scalar curl at the point $(0,-1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})}_{(0,-1)} & =\frac{2(0)(-1)}{{0}^{2}+1}-2(-1) \\  & =0+2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

q-126537:
